reasoning:
The claim that MSG causes "Chinese restaurant syndrome" (including symptoms like headaches and numbness) has been thoroughly debunked by scientific research. The term originated from a single speculative letter written by a physician to the New England Journal of Medicine in 1968. Since then, numerous rigorous, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies have failed to find any consistent or causal link between MSG consumption and these symptoms in the general public. 

Furthermore, major health and food safety organizations, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), classify MSG as "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS). The glutamate in MSG is chemically indistinguishable from the glutamate naturally found in foods like tomatoes, cheese, and mushrooms, which do not trigger similar complaints.
